q: During craniotomy the brain is tight. Which measure is appropriate?
o: Osmotherapy, brief mild hyperventilation and deepening TIVA
why: Brain relaxation: mannitol or hypertonic saline, brief hyperventilation, deepen anaesthesia, head up and keep venous drainage free.

q: What volatile concentration is generally used if a volatile is chosen for craniotomy?
why: Below 1 MAC limits cerebral vasodilatation and rises in CBF and ICP.

q: How is hypertension at head pinning prevented?
o: Local anaesthetic infiltration or a remifentanil bolus before pinning
why: Pinning is very stimulating; prepare with LA or remifentanil.

q: Which is NOT part of normal physiology targets during craniotomy?
why: Aim for normocapnia, normothermia and normoglycaemia; hyperglycaemia worsens ischaemic injury.

q: Why are NSAIDs a relative contraindication after neurosurgery?
why: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk; analgesia uses scalp block, paracetamol, codeine or small morphine doses.

q: What is the first step in assessing delayed recovery after GA?
why: Steps: neuro assessment, ABG, review the anaesthetic chart, consider reversal, then CT head.

q: What are the components of the normal ICP waveform?
o: P1 percussion (arterial), P2 tidal (compliance), P3 dicrotic
why: A rising P2 above P1 suggests reduced compliance; A (plateau) waves indicate critically reduced compliance.

q: What is the normal adult ICP?
A third nerve palsy with raised ICP suggests which herniation?
why: Uncal herniation compresses CN III; a sixth nerve palsy is a false localising sign.

q: Why is a smooth emergence without coughing important after craniotomy?
o: Coughing and hypertension raise ICP and risk haematoma
why: Avoid coughing and hypertension at emergence; early neuro assessment follows.
